readings.title: Labels on a packing line
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A small factory packed household goods. Several boxes left with the wrong size label even though workers checked each package. The main obstacle was similar labels stored side by side. Two size codes differed by one small letter and looked alike under the line lighting. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a review of error times and label placement. Supervisors traced when mistakes occurred and observed the choice without blaming workers. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated layout contributed more than worker speed. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced separate label trays and clearer type. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: quality problems often begin in process design. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in labels on a packing line, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Training for a new measuring tool
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A workshop purchased a digital measuring tool. Experienced workers used it confidently, but results varied between shifts. The main obstacle was different calibration habits. The display looked ready before a required setup step had been completed. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a comparison of shift procedures. A technician observed the same sample being measured under each routine. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated consistent setup reduced variation. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a brief shared calibration checklist. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: reliable measurement depends on a common method. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in training for a new measuring tool, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Finding damage during delivery
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A furniture maker received complaints about scratched tables. Inspection records showed the surfaces were clean before packing. The main obstacle was damage occurring after final inspection. Several tables travelled in boxes with loose protective corners. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used photographs at packing and arrival. The team compared transport conditions and asked drivers when packages shifted. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated box movement caused repeated marks. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced better corner supports and a packing check. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: quality extends beyond the factory door. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in finding damage during delivery, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A suggestion board that gets answers
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Employees posted improvement ideas on a factory board. After months without replies, fewer workers used it. The main obstacle was suggestions without visible follow-up. Staff could not tell whether an idea was rejected, delayed or being tried. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a review of submissions and decision dates. Managers grouped ideas by type and spoke with workers about the response they expected. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated timely explanations kept participation alive. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a dated status and short reason for every suggestion. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: listening requires an answer as well as a form. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a suggestion board that gets answers, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful plan for manufacturing and quality improvement must take account of the people who will use it. An idea may look complete on paper and still create difficulties during an ordinary week. Organizers therefore tried the small factory improvement programme on a small scale and invited comments from users with different schedules. They recorded benefits as well as the time and resources needed to provide them. Some findings supported the original aim, while others suggested that the method should change. The group published both kinds of result instead of presenting the trial as a simple success or failure. This allowed residents to discuss the next step with a clearer understanding of its possible effects.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 关于制造业与质量改进的有用方案必须考虑实际使用它的人。一个想法在纸上看似完整，平常使用时却仍可能出现困难。因此，组织者小规模试行该服务，并邀请时间安排不同的使用者提出意见。他们既记录益处，也记录提供这些益处所需的时间和资源。有些发现支持最初目标，另一些则表明方法应当调整。团队同时公布两类结果，而没有把试行简单说成成功或失败。这让居民能更清楚地了解可能的影响，再讨论下一步。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the quality improvement team about a community activity related to manufacturing and quality improvement. Explain how different people can participate, what should be recorded, and how the results should be shared.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the small factory improvement programme. People have noticed similar labels stored side by side, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
